Chapter 9: Self-Advocacy and the Ongoing Journey
Even when the load is shared and that pressure to be perfect finally starts to ease up, the journey isn’t really over, is it? Old habits and expectations—well, they have a sneaky way of slipping back in, especially when life gets hectic.
That’s why self-advocacy—speaking up for what you need, setting boundaries, and asking for help—turns out to be a lifelong practice, not just a one-and-done thing.
Picture this: there’s a parent who, during a busy season, starts noticing those old patterns creeping back. The to-do list keeps growing, and suddenly, she feels that urge to handle everything herself. But this time? She catches it. She pauses, takes a deep breath, and asks her partner to take care of dinner. It might seem like a small step, but honestly, it makes all the difference.
Now, let’s shift to the workplace. Maybe you’ve been that person who always says “yes” to every request. But now, before agreeing, you stop and check in with yourself: “Do I actually have the capacity for this?” Sometimes, the answer is no—and you know what? That’s okay. The guilt might still be there, but it’s softer now, a little easier to handle.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most people don’t realize self-advocacy isn’t a single moment. It’s a skill you keep practicing, with patience and a bit of self-kindness. There’ll be setbacks, moments of doubt, and days when it feels simpler to just take it all on. But each time you speak up, set a boundary, or reach out for help, the path forward gets a bit clearer.
The truth is, this journey toward equity and self-care never really ends. There’s no finish line—no perfect moment where everything is balanced just right. Instead, it’s a series of choices, day after day, each one giving you a chance to build a life that feels fair and fulfilling.
And as self-advocacy becomes more of a habit, something shifts. You start feeling more confident, more clear-headed, and there’s just a little more space to breathe. The responsibilities are still there, but now, they’re chosen—not just expected.
Before long, it gets easier to ask for what you need—and just as important, to offer that same support to the people around you.
